### 2026-11-08: # November 5, 6, 7, 8: The Whole Thing!

# November 5, 6, 7, 8: The Whole Thing!

For the sake of time (only 1 hour left!), I decided to just make the whole project one devlog to make things go quicker. My project for this week is an e-paper checklist that'll help me be more organized. I initially wanted to use a rotary encoder, but I landed on using three buttons instead just to make things easier to design and control. I decided on using e-paper because it retains what it displays, even when the device is turned off. This means that you'll be able to turn the device only when you need to check/uncheck an item, which will make the device last a long time on one charge.

## November 5: Schematic (2 hrs)
I went with the XIAO ESP32-S3 again for this project because I already have a lot of experience with using it from the Virtual Sandbox. It also has some solder pads at the bottom so I can easily add a battery.

For the e-paper screen, I decided to use one that talks over SPI so I can simply add pins to the board rather than a whole ribbon cable connection. Following a wiring diagram, I connected all of the screen's pins to an appropriate place on the ESP32.

I added three buttons: one to move up, one to move down, and one to confirm a check/uncheck action. Each one got a 10k pull-up resistor, which I already have from an Arduino kit.

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.27.49 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/ed8bc9c95edfaae72cb0e689357c08a475c6107cc2b4241ec9371038c4de907d.png)

For the battery, I copied the same setup I used for the Virtual Sandbox, where I added two 1x1 connectors and added an on/off switch in the middle, that way the switch can be securely soldered onto the PCB. The ERC was giving me an error, so I searched up how to troubleshoot, so the last thing I did was add a power flag on ground.

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.28.32 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/a2aa7a532eaf3f405a4950818cf4be5f8ead8442139cc488f83e90ad9f7e8c89.png)

##  November 6-7: PCB, BOM, and Github (4 hrs for PCB, 3 for BOM and Github)
The final board was 96x60 mm so it stays under the 100x100 mm limit for a cheaper priced board. The screen covers most of the front of the board, and the three buttons are underneath.The ESP32, switch, pull-up resistors, and capacitors are on the back. I was sure to leave some extra space for the battery, so I did a rough outline of where I wanted it and will add some double-sided tape to mount it in place.

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.38.28 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/1d584354e4dbbbc5ba5d66630309cd5d9bb78b1b8f0d9b558ab7dd3c6c46e356.png)
I had to redo the PCB and schematic a couple times because I was going back and forth between two screens I found while doing my BOM. One of the screens had a 1x8 connector, and the other had a 2x4 connector. I originally had the 1x8, but I found the 2x4 for cheaper, so I redid the work to account for that. Later, I found out that with shipping, the 2x4 screen is more expensive, so I switched back to the 1x8 connector. I also had to get rid of the screw holes because the dimensions weren't listed on the listing, so I plan to fix the screen in place using some more double-sided tape.

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.39.34 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/6c6eba23716780b6b0184d81c482217b2bedee00300ecb2120e5bf7098cd4ba9.png)

While doing the BOM, I realized that I could save costs by replacing the resistors and capacitors with the types I already have, so I replaced the footprints for the generic components that I have in my Arduino kit and retouched the PCB. I finalized the board with some small touch-ups to the silkscreen until the DRC said there were zero errors. The whole thing stays pretty true to my original design.

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.40.54 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/c13227d5a49a4880ed23e72dcb3961c1916b1d2bb7fc0a4bb02215ff1d7ff0b3.png)

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.41.00 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/04928cd87744784493cf95462757c208dbc01b629b1cb745f7994d17180d76af.png)

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.37.56 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/b26032774b99ff645fc53ac3bf98532892b99aae0f74a16871acf42bdb9a2ace.png)

The BOM was a bit annoying because I was doing all my shopping on AIiExpress, so I had to find items with cheap/no shipping to keep costs down. After adding all the components I needed, I was able to cut some stuff because I'll already be buying them for previous weeks, so I'll have some extras for this project. Ultimately, I ended up buying four items: the PCB, the ESP32-S3, the 2.9" e-paper screen, and the LiPo battery. The costs totaled pretty well thanks to a great coupon from JLCPCB.

![Screenshot 2026-11-08 at 11.44.53 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/280c114d4f6a20a546dde3d9f634989a94f02a645f04a18fe49f88cbba54f093.png)

Then, I added the production files, schematic, and PCB to the GitHub repo. My files got a bit messy, so it took some time to find the files I needed to add to the repo.

## November 7-8: Doing the Firmware (4 hrs)
I wrote the firmware in Arduino C++ using the GxEPD2 library. UP and DOWN move a black highlight bar through the list, OK checks/unchecks the highlighted item, and holding DOWN for 1.5 seconds unchecks everything so I can start fresh the next day. The header shows how many items are done, which page I'm on, and the battery percentage.

The hardest part was getting sleep to work the way I wanted. After 4 seconds with no presses, the board goes into sleep mode, and any of the three buttons wakes it up. Waking up basically restarts the ESP32, so at first a press would just wake it without doing anything. I fixed that by checking which button woke it and running that button's action right away, so one tap works even from sleep. I also learned that normal variables get wiped during sleep, so the highlighted item is stored in RTC memory and the checkmarks are saved to flash. I used AI to polish up my code/UI and remove errors, especially with the GxEPD2 library.

I hardcoded the list of activities that need to be completed, but in the future I want to create some sort of app or web page that allows you to edit the list from another device like a phone or computer.

The final product looks good to me, and I hope it'll help me stay more organized with my time!

# tl;dr: I designed, routed, and programmed an e-paper checklist device that helps me stay organized. I redid the PCB a couple times because I had to replace footprints for the e-paper display, capacitor, and resistors. The firmware allows you to check/uncheck items on your list. In the future, I want to add a way to edit the list, because right now it's just hardcoded.
